name: Nd:YAG laser hair removal

card.summary: The 1064 nm laser used for hair reduction on darker skin tones, with deeper penetration and less surface melanin absorption.
card.note: Reduction rather than guaranteed removal; usually more sessions on fine or light hair.

quick.overview:
Nd:YAG lasers emit infrared light at 1064 nm. Wikipedia lists this wavelength as the one for dark skin in hair removal, and a 2022 prospective study said alexandrite and Nd:YAG are the most effective options in lighter and darker skin phototypes respectively.

Studies of fluence and histology in the early 2000s examined millisecond Nd:YAG lasers for hair removal.
quick.mechanism: Selective photothermolysis: the longer wavelength is absorbed less by skin pigment and penetrates deeper, targeting hair-follicle melanin while sparing the surface better in darker skin.
quick.risks: Redness, swelling, pain, burns and pigment change are possible; the general risks Wikipedia lists for laser hair removal apply.

lead: Nd:YAG laser hair removal uses a 1064 nm neodymium-doped yttrium aluminium garnet laser to reduce dark hair. It is the laser Wikipedia lists for hair removal in dark skin. [1] People use it to get smoother, hair-free skin on the face, jawline, neck, chest, back, arms and legs, so that skin looks cleaner and, for those who shave, free of stubble, razor bumps and ingrown hairs, without repeated shaving or waxing.

Its appeal for darker skin comes from the wavelength. Melanin absorbs shorter wavelengths strongly, which can leave the pigment in the skin surface competing with the pigment in the hair. At 1064 nm, melanin absorption in the skin is minimal and the light penetrates deeper, so a 2005 review described the long-pulsed Nd:YAG as the safest hair-removal device for dark-skinned patients. [9][13] Alexandrite, diode, ruby and intense pulsed light devices are the other common options and are generally paired with lighter skin. [1][9]

Bell Laboratories first demonstrated Nd:YAG laser operation in 1964, and the laser is used in cosmetic medicine for hair removal and for minor vascular defects. [2] Published human studies include fluence comparisons and histology from 2001, a systematic review of 13 trials with 734 patients, and a 2022 prospective study comparing traditional and in-motion techniques. [3][4][5][10]

chain: 1064 nm light is absorbed by melanin in the hair follicle
Follicle is heated and its growth is reduced over a series of sessions
Fewer or finer regrowing hairs, less shaving and fewer razor bumps
angle.text: Nd:YAG treatment reduces the number of regrowing dark hairs in the treated area, which people use to keep the face, neck, body and bikini line smooth. The long wavelength is the one clinics typically choose for darker skin tones. [1][9]

infobox: Used for dark skin; 1064 nm also treats types I to VI [13]
Eight or more sessions, three to eight weeks apart [1]

paras: Laser hair removal relies on selective photothermolysis, a concept developed by R. Rox Anderson and Melanie Grossman: a wavelength and pulse duration are chosen so that light is absorbed by a specific target, here the melanin in the hair, which heats the follicle's stem cells while sparing most of the surrounding skin. Commercial systems appeared in 1995 to 1996 and the US FDA cleared the approach in 1997. [1]

Within the family of hair-removal lasers, Wikipedia lists alexandrite at 755 nm, diode at 810 nm, ruby at 694 nm and Nd:YAG at 1064 nm, with Nd:YAG assigned to dark skin. [1] A 2005 review noted that the older devices all give roughly 75 percent hair reduction in light skin (phototypes I to III), whereas the long wavelength of the Nd:YAG makes it the safest choice for dark-skinned patients. [9]

A 2023 study measured how the temperature of hair samples changed under alexandrite and Nd:YAG hair-removal pulses, in order to describe the photothermal process, including a rapid rise in hair temperature during the pulse. [6] Histologic work in 2001 on six patients with black hair examined the thermal effect on follicles after 50 millisecond pulses at fluences of 30, 50 and 100 J/cm2. [5]

Because lasers only affect follicles in the active growth phase, treatment is delivered as a series. Wikipedia states that most people need at least eight sessions spaced three to eight weeks apart, and that touch-ups may be needed. [1]

Laser hair removal was experimental for roughly two decades before the first commercial systems arrived in 1995 to 1996. A 1998 article from the Massachusetts General Hospital group was among the first published accounts of the method, and the US FDA cleared the approach in 1997.[1] The scientific basis was selective photothermolysis, worked out by R. Rox Anderson and Melanie Grossman, in which light is matched to a target pigment so that follicle stem cells are heated while neighbouring skin is spared.[1]

The Nd:YAG (neodymium-doped yttrium aluminium garnet) laser emits at 1064 nm and was adapted for hair removal because that long wavelength is absorbed less by epidermal melanin than shorter wavelengths, which is why it became the device associated with darker skin types.[1][2]

Operators set the spot size (roughly 3 to 18 mm on typical devices) and the fluence, measured in joules per square centimetre, and the pulse duration is chosen so the follicle stays hot long enough to be damaged.[1] Cooling is built into most systems: a chilled contact window, a cryogen spray or forced air at around minus 34 degrees Celsius. Cooling allows higher fluences and reduces discomfort and side effects, particularly in darker skin.[1]

Discomfort is expected. Clinics may offer topical numbing cream, often applied around 30 minutes beforehand, and icing afterwards is commonly used; Wikipedia notes that strong numbing creams over large areas carry their own risks.[1] Treated hairs usually shed over two to three weeks, and the article states that pulling them out can be more painful and may reduce results.[1]

Because lasers act on follicles in the active growth phase, treatment is a series. Most people need at least eight sessions spaced about three to eight weeks apart depending on the body area, men's facial hair often needs considerably more, and touch-ups may follow on large areas.[1]

In the United States the FDA regulates the manufacture and sale of the devices but there is no federal licensing for practitioners; nearly all states regulate for-hire services, with rules ranging from physician-only supervision to allowing licensed nurses, estheticians or cosmetologists.[1] The FDA defines permanent hair reduction as a long-term, stable reduction in the number of regrowing hairs rather than complete removal.[1] As of 2025 Wikipedia lists two diode devices cleared for over-the-counter sale, the Epilaser and the TRIA; Nd:YAG devices are professional equipment.[1]

People seek Nd:YAG hair removal for unwanted facial and body hair, for the beard line and neck, and for areas where shaving causes ingrown hairs or irritation. Because 1064 nm penetrates deeper, clinics also use it on skin that tans easily or is darker, where other wavelengths carry more pigment risk. [9][13]

Wikipedia notes that laser hair removal works best on dark, coarse hair, and that it responds poorly to white, grey, light blonde, red and fine vellus hair. The Nd:YAG is stated to treat black hair on darker skin with some success. [1] Devices cleared by the FDA are labelled for permanent hair reduction, meaning a long-term, stable reduction in regrowing hairs rather than complete removal. [1]

A 2001 study of 15 subjects compared long-pulsed Nd:YAG fluences of 50, 80 and 100 J/cm2 for efficacy and safety. [3] A 2022 prospective study of 40 patients with skin types 2 to 6 divided them into two groups, one treated with the traditional technique and one with an in-motion technique, and noted that alexandrite and Nd:YAG are considered the most effective lasers in lighter and darker phototypes respectively. [4]

A 2020 systematic review of randomized trials of 1064 nm photoepilation included 13 articles covering 734 patients and concluded that the laser shows safety and promising beneficial effects for hair removal, while calling for further scientific work. [10] A randomized trial of blended 755/1064 nm laser energy has also been published. [11]

Researchers are also looking at whether 1064 nm treatment can change hair shaft diameter: a small completed study of 14 participants with androgenetic alopecia registered optimization of long-pulsed Nd:YAG parameters for this purpose. [12]

Wikipedia lists redness, swelling and itching lasting two or three days as the usual after-effects of laser hair removal. More serious risks include acne flares, discoloration of the skin, and, rarely, burns, scarring and infection. Numbing creams used over large areas carry their own risks. [1]
Pigment change and burns are the concerns most often raised for people with darker skin, which is the reason the longer 1064 nm wavelength is selected for them. [9][13]

Human studies include the 2001 fluence comparison in 15 subjects [3], the histologic evaluation of a millisecond Nd:YAG laser in six patients [5], the 2022 in-motion comparison in 40 patients [4], the 2020 systematic review of 13 trials [10] and a randomized trial of blended 755/1064 nm energy [11].

Registered trials use laser hair removal as a medical treatment for pilonidal disease, including a 302-participant study and a pilot in patients with darker skin, and for hidradenitis suppurativa. [7][8][14]

timeline.event: Nd:YAG laser operation first demonstrated at Bell Laboratories. [2]
Laser hair removal becomes commercially available after about 20 years of testing. [1]
The US FDA approves the laser hair-removal approach. [1]
Studies of millisecond Nd:YAG hair removal published on fluence and follicle histology. [3][5]
A review names long-pulsed Nd:YAG as the safest hair-removal laser for dark-skinned patients. [9]
Systematic review of 13 trials of 1064 nm photoepilation published. [10]
Prospective study compares traditional and in-motion Nd:YAG technique. [4]
